newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Zaire refugees' food stocks low, UN seeks flights.
newsitem.headline: Zaire refugees' food stocks low, UN seeks flights.

text.p: The 200,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire, trapped in the middle of fighting between Zairean troops and rebels, are down to only a week of U.N. food suppplies, the United Nations refugee agency said on Tuesday.

Assisting the refugees, in Lubutu region some 240 km (150 miles) southeast of Zaire's regional capital Kisangani, has become a logistical nightmare for aid agencies with fighting between Tutsi-led rebels and troops moving closer.

The UNHCR said it was negotiating with Zairean authorities, who barred foreign aid flights from landing directly at Kisangani, for permission to use the airport at the regional hub, also the base for Zaire's army counter-offensive.

"It is desperately important to get agreement on this," UNHCR spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole told a news briefing. "If flights have to go through Kinshasha, it's much more time-consuming, much more costly. The whole process slows down.

The UNHCR said food convoys, which had been delayed three to four days, arrived in the region on Monday, and distribution of rations has begun for the three camps holding the refugees -- Tingi-Tingi (120,000), Amisi (40,000) and Shabunda (40,000).
"But at the moment food stocks are very low. Unless aid flights are allowed, the situation will deteriorate rapidly within a very short time," spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said.

"According to one of representatives on the ground, the food that has been distributed already will only last around a week. And we will have nothing left to distribute unless something is done about allowing aid flights in," she told a news briefing.
She was quoting UNHCR's officer in charge in the area, Dillah Doumaye, who referred to World Food Programme stocks.

Sadako Ogata, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, leaves on Thursday for a trip to Africa's Great Lakes region, beginning with talks with Zairean officials in Kinshasha on Friday, to seek ways of increasing the amount of aid getting into eastern Zaire and ways of assuring the safety of refugees.

Ogata spoke at length on Monday with Emma Bonino, the Eruopean Union commissioner who described conditions at Zaire's largest remaining refugee camp for Hutus as beneath human dignity and said the world should be ashamed.
"They agreed on the need for political action to help the humanitarian agencies carry out their work on the ground," the UNHCR spokeswoman said.
The immediate task was to provide sufficient assistance for the refugees, lower the mortality rates in the camps and build up the refugees' strength so they can return to their homeland.
O'Toole said refugees in Tingi-Tingi were dying at a rate of 20 a day from malnutrition and disease and 64 died in the past week in Amisi where causes included malaria and malnutrition.

The main concern at moment was Punia, about 160 km (100 miles) north of Shabunda on the way to Lubuto. A joint UNHCR/UNICEF mission has visited Punia, where there are an estimated 20,000 refugees and internally-displaced.
Food requirement for all three camps is 100 metric tonnes a day, but only half of that has been getting through, UNHCR said.

"It is extremely difficult to work out how to help these people. It appears almost impossible to set up another refugee site in eastern Zaire because of lack of resources and logistical problems," O'Toole said.

"On the other hand, if nothing is done, these people might die on the spot or in the forest. The situation is extremely volatile in the region...The security situation isn't really conducive to starting anything immediate (on repatriation)."
